class.name: WeatherRainEffect
class.brief_description: Rain for a [Weather] node: raindrops, impacts and a rain occlusion map.
class.description: Rains around the camera as much as [method Weather.get_rain_amount] says, slanted by the wind. Drops are lit, see-through streaks that refract the scene and reflect the sky's light ([method Weather.get_horizon_light]), so rain shows against dark ground under clouds. Where a drop hits geometry, an impact draws a ring (on wet surfaces), a crown of droplets and a thin cup of water. Only a box of [member area_size] around the camera is simulated, by [GPUParticles3D] with a [GPUParticlesCollisionHeightField3D] that follows the camera, so drops stop on the first surface they hit: no rain under roofs. The rain amount scales the live particle count, so changes never restart the rain. The particle counts and map sizes follow [member Weather.quality]. The rain occlusion map is a top-down height map around the camera, re-rendered only after moving [member occlusion_update_step] and only while something is wet. Wet surface shaders ([code]res://.builtin/wet_surface.gdshader[/code], or [code]weather_apply_wetness()[/code] from [code]res://.builtin/weather_wetness.gdshaderinc[/code]) compare each surface with the highest cover above it, so the ground under roofs, overhangs and tables stays dry. It is passed in the global shader parameters [code]weather_rain_occlusion[/code] and [code]weather_occlusion_area[/code]. The nodes are internal children of the [Weather] node and are never saved.

method.name: get_max_drops
method.description: The number of drops at full rain, set by the quality level.

method.name: get_max_impacts
method.description: The number of impacts at full rain, set by the quality level.

method.name: get_occlusion_area
method.description: The area the occlusion map covers: center x and z, width in meters, and [code]1.0[/code] in w while the map is in use ([code]Vector4(0, 0, 0, 0)[/code] when it isn't). The same value as the [code]weather_occlusion_area[/code] global shader parameter.

method.name: get_occlusion_texture
method.description: The occlusion map: the height in meters of the highest surface above each point, in the red channel. [code]null[/code] when the effect isn't running or [member occlusion_enabled] is off.

method.name: refresh_occlusion
method.description: Renders the occlusion map again now, for example after building or moving a cover. Otherwise it is only rendered after the camera moves [member occlusion_update_step].

members.member: Width of the box around the camera where it rains, in meters. Rain further away is the haze's job.

Seconds between captures of the collision height field while it rains, even when the camera doesn't move, so moved objects (doors, vehicles, pushed props) don't leave invisible surfaces that drops splash on. [code]0.0[/code] captures only after moving.
Render layers that count as cover for the occlusion map. The rain's own layers are left out.
Height above the camera where drops start, in meters.
Speed of the falling drops, in meters per second. Real raindrops fall at 5 to 9 m/s; a little faster reads better on screen.
If [code]true[/code], each impact also puffs a faint spray. Off by default: single puffs tend to look like snowflakes.
If [code]true[/code], drops that hit geometry splash. The splashes are a sub-emitter of the drops.
Width of the occlusion map, in meters. Surfaces outside it are always exposed to the rain.
Height above the camera from which the occlusion map is captured, in meters. Covers higher than this don't count.
If [code]true[/code], surfaces under cover stay dry. Without it, wet surface shaders treat everything as open to the sky.
The occlusion map is rendered again after the camera moves this far, in meters. Its position snaps to this grid, so it never shimmers.
Render layers of the drops and impacts. The collision height field and the occlusion map ignore these layers.
How bright the sky's light looks in the drops.
Length of a drop's streak, in meters: a camera exposure smears each drop into a line.
Width of a drop's streak, in meters. Far drops are never drawn thinner than a pixel and a half; they get fainter instead.
How much of the wind's speed the drops take on. Drops nearly reach the wind's speed in a fraction of a second.
